glossary.Adrenal insufficiency: The adrenal glands do not make enough steroid hormones.
glossary.Stress response: The body's hormonal reaction to illness or injury, including a rise in cortisol.
glossary.Electrolyte: A salt in the blood such as sodium or potassium.
glossary.Mineralocorticoids: Steroid hormones, mainly aldosterone, that control salt and water balance.
glossary.Glucocorticoids: Steroid hormones, mainly cortisol, that affect metabolism, immunity and the stress response.
glossary.TB: Tuberculosis, a bacterial infection that can destroy the adrenal glands.
glossary.Opportunistic infections: Infections that take hold mainly when immunity is weak, as in HIV.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which weakens the immune system.
glossary.Infiltrative: Describes diseases where abnormal material builds up in and damages an organ.
glossary.Amyloidosis: Build-up of abnormal folded protein (amyloid) in organs.
glossary.Sarcoidosis: Disease with clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomas) in many organs.
glossary.Exogenous steroids: Steroid medicines given from outside the body, which can suppress the adrenals.
glossary.Type 1 diabetes: Autoimmune destruction of insulin-making cells in the pancreas.
glossary.Shock: Blood pressure too low to supply the organs adequately.
glossary.Physiological stress: Illness, injury or surgery that raises the body's need for cortisol.
glossary.Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage: Bleeding into both adrenal glands, destroying them suddenly.
glossary.ACTH stimulation test: Giving synthetic ACTH and measuring whether cortisol rises.
glossary.Serum cortisol: Cortisol level measured in a blood sample.
glossary.Tertiary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure due to lack of CRH from the hypothalamus.
glossary.Autoantibodies: Antibodies made against the body's own proteins.
glossary.Glucocorticoid replacement: Giving steroid tablets to replace missing cortisol.
glossary.Intercurrent illness: A new illness happening on top of an existing condition.
glossary.Resuscitation: Urgent treatment to restore circulation, such as fast IV fluids.
glossary.0.9% saline: Salt solution given into a vein to restore fluid volume.
glossary.Negative feedback: When a hormone switches off the signal that produced it; low cortisol releases this brake.
glossary.Melanocyte-stimulating hormone: Hormone that makes skin pigment cells produce melanin.
glossary.Precursor: A larger molecule that is cut up to make smaller active molecules.
glossary.Reabsorption: Taking substances back from urine into the blood in the kidney.
glossary.Volume depletion: Loss of fluid from the circulation, lowering blood pressure.
glossary.Vascular tone: The degree of tightening of blood vessel walls, which maintains blood pressure.
glossary.Refractory hypotension: Low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids.
glossary.Stress-dose steroids: Higher steroid doses given during illness or surgery to copy the normal cortisol surge.
glossary.Adrenal gland imaging: CT or MRI of the adrenal glands to look for infection, bleeding or tumour.
